details:
**Eliza Doolittle**
She is the Cockney flower girl at the centre of the play, and she is trained to speak and behave like a lady. At an embassy reception, Higgins's former pupil Nepommuck, a Hungarian interpreter, wrongly declares that she is a Hungarian princess of "royal blood."

**Henry Higgins and Colonel Pickering's bet**
Henry Higgins is a professor of phonetics who lives on Wimpole Street. Colonel Pickering wrote "Spoken Sanskrit" and studies Indian dialects. The two men bet on whether Higgins can make Eliza speak well enough to pass her off as a duchess. The play is named after the sculptor in Greek myth who fell in love with his own statue, and it was adapted into the musical and film *My Fair Lady*.

**Freddy Eynsford-Hill**
He is a weak but kind young gentleman who bumps into Eliza and her flowers in Covent Garden. He falls for her when he meets her again later. Eliza decides to marry Freddy instead of staying with Higgins.

**Covent Garden opening scene and the Note-Taker**
Act One takes place in the rain under the portico of a church in Covent Garden, London's market district. Higgins, listed as "The Note-Taker," writes down people's speech and guesses where they come from by their accents. Eliza ("The Flower Girl") fears he is a police informer and cries, "I'm a good girl, I am." Other characters in the scene include "The Sarcastic Bystander" and "The Gentleman" (Pickering).

**"Most original moralist" and the Wannafeller Moral Reform World League**
As a joke, Higgins writes to the American millionaire Ezra D. Wannafeller that Eliza's father, Alfred Doolittle, is "the most original moralist" in England. Wannafeller dies and leaves Doolittle money in his will on condition that he gives lectures for the Wannafeller Moral Reform World League. This makes Doolittle unhappily respectable, trapped by "middle-class morality."

**The thrown slippers**
After Eliza's triumph at the embassy party, Higgins ignores her and takes all the credit. When he asks where his slippers are, she throws them at him, calls him a selfish brute, and asks why he didn't leave her in the gutter.

**"Not bloody likely!"**
When Freddy asks Eliza if she is walking across the park, she gives this shocking answer during a visit to Higgins's mother's home. The line caused a sensation in 1914, and "Not Pygmalion likely" became a joking substitute for the swear word.

**"What Happened Afterwards" and Herbert Beerbohm Tree**
Herbert Beerbohm Tree played Higgins in the first London production and suggested that Higgins and Eliza would end up together. Shaw, the author, objected and added a prose epilogue called "What Happened Afterwards." It says Eliza marries Freddy and opens a flower shop with money from Pickering, and that she studies bookkeeping and typewriting to keep it running. It also says that Freddy's sister Clara starts reading the novels of H. G. Wells.

**"The new small talk"**
At Mrs. Higgins's "at-home" (an afternoon reception), Eliza speaks with perfect pronunciation but uses gutter phrases. She claims her aunt was "done in" by relatives and says gin was "mother's milk" to her. Higgins passes this off as "the new small talk," and Freddy's sister Clara is impressed enough to copy it.

**Mrs. Higgins ("Men! Men! Men!")**
She is Henry's sensible mother. She teases him that he never falls in love with anyone under forty-five, and she later shelters Eliza when Eliza runs away from him. Act Three ends with her exasperated cry "Men! Men! Men!" at how thoughtless Higgins and Pickering are.

**Mrs. Pearce, the bath, and the kimono**
Mrs. Pearce is Higgins's housekeeper. She scrubs Eliza in a bath while Eliza screams, and Eliza is so embarrassed by the bathroom mirror that she covers it. Afterwards, Eliza is dressed in a blue Japanese kimono.

**Alfred Doolittle sells his daughter for five pounds**
Eliza's father, a dustman, comes to Higgins's house to get money for his daughter. He takes five pounds and refuses ten. When Pickering asks, "Have you no morals, man?", he replies that he can't afford them.

**The chocolates**
To tempt Eliza into lessons, Higgins pops a chocolate into her mouth to silence her. Because she suspects it is poisoned, he eats half of one to prove it is safe.

**The ring in the fireplace**
During their fight after the embassy party, Eliza gives back a ring Higgins bought her. He angrily throws it into the fireplace, and she later looks for it.

**"Ah-ah-ah-ow-ow-oo!"**
This is Eliza's typical Cockney howl of protest. She "relapses" into it when her father unexpectedly comes in from the balcony near the end of the play, which shows that her new speech is not yet second nature.
